full_judgment:
Abdul Bari Sarker, J.: This Rule arises out of an application under section 561A of the Code of Criminal Procedure for quashing the Petition Case No. 345A-1/89, pending in the Court of Chief Metropolitan Magistrate, Dhaka under section 108 (2) of the Companies Act, 1913. 

 2. The facts of the case are that the opposite party No. 1 Makbul Ahmed filed a petition of complaint before the Chief Metropolitan Magistrate against the five petitioners and two others stating that the accused persons arc the directors of M/s. Nahar Shipping Lines Ltd., a Public Ltd. Company with registered Head Office at Red Cross Chamber, 3rd floor, 87, Motijheel Commercial Area, Dhaka and the total share capital of that company is 1,24,00,000/=. The value of each share is Tk. 100/=. It is further stated that the complainant on the declaration of the company, offering sale of shares purchased 1000 shares and deposited its value of Tk. 1,00,000/= to accused No. 2, Mrs. Syeda Serajun Nahar, the Managing Director of the Company on receipt of the receipt. The Company showed allotment of 1000 shares in favour of the complainant in the meeting of the Board of the Company held on 31.3.80 and accordingly submitted return to the Registrar of the Company. The accused persons, however, did not issue any share certificates to him for his 1000 shares in spite of the fact that it is compulsory for the accused persons to issue the share certificates to the complainant as per the provision of section 108 of the Companies Act in spite of repeated demands made by the complainant. Later on the accused persons informed the complainant that they mortgaged the shares of the complainant to the BSRS for raising a loan. The complainant raised objection stating that he did not consent to mortgage his shares to the BSRS and it was done without his knowledge. As a dispute arose regarding the matter, it was referred to an Arbitration consisting of two members as per Article 218 of the Article of the Constitution. As the members differed in their opinion, the case was referred to an umpire and the umpire held that the shares of the complainant was mortgaged to BSRS without his consent and the umpire directed the accused to deliver the share certificates to the complainant within 15 days from 22.6.85, in default, the complainant could approach the Court to obtain a Rule to the above effect. But as the accused persons did not comply with the direction of the Umpire, the Umpire referred the matter to the learned Subordinate Judge, 3rd Court, Dhaka in Arbitration Case No. 710 of 1985 and the Court by order dated 31.8.86 made the decision of the umpire as the rule of the Court and directed the accused persons to deliver the share certificates to the complainant within 15 days. The company however, preferred appeal No 256 of 1987 in the Supreme Court, High Court Division and the High Court Division by its decision on 31.3.88 confirmed the order of the learned Subordinate Judge and dismissed the appeal. The company then approached the Appellate Division in Civil Petition Case No.96 of 1988 against the decision of the High Court Division and the Appellate Division dismissed the CP. Case and upheld the decision of the High Court Division. Even after the decision of the Appellate Division, the accused persons did not deliver the share certificates to the complainant. On the contrary in letter dated 12.3.89, they expressed their inability to deliver their share certificates and offered the value of the certificates to the complainant but the complainant by a letter dated 23.3.89 informed them that he does not want the value of the shares but wanted the share certificates as per the decision of the Court. But in spite of that the accused persons did not deliver the share certificates to the complainant and thereby committed an offence punishable under section 108 (2) of the Companies Act and filed the above petition of complaint. 

 4. Dr. Rafiqur Rahman, the learned Counsel for the petitioners, has taken us through the facts of the case. He contends that section 108(2) of the Companies Act does not contemplate any offence for non-delivery of the share certificates and as such the present case is a misconceived one and is liable to be quashed. 

 6. Dr. Rahman argues that section 108(1) contemplates that the share certificates must be complete and ready for delivery within three months from the date of allotment or transfer of the shares and if the shares are complete and made ready for delivery within three months the obligation of the company is over and it does not extend to the actual delivery of the same to the share-holders. In support of his contention he referred to and relied on a decision made in the case of Asiatic Oxygen Ltd. reported in AIR 1972 (Cal) page 50 at page 52. In paragraph 8 it was observed as follows: 

 "8. The failure to comply with the requirements of sub-section (1) to the said section thus shall be visited with penal consequences. In that view of the matter, in my opinion, the said sub-section has to be construed strictly (See AIR) 52 (SC) 156; See also Maxwell on Interpretation of Statutes 11th Edition pages 254-55). The said subsection nowhere provides for delivery of the certificates of share or debentures or debenture stocks but only enjoins upon the company to have the same ready for delivery. The said words in the sub-section, in my opinion should not be construed in such a way as to give an extended meaning to the words "to have them ready for delivery". The sub-section (1) does not impose an obligation upon the Company to deliver the said share, etc. Thus, in my opinion, sub-section (3) to the said section does not authorise a person to have an order for delivery of the said share. In that view of the matter, in my opinion, this application is misconceived and must fail." 

 7. In that case an application under section 113 of the Companies Act, 1956 (of India) was made for directing the Company to deliver the share certificates to the petitioners who purchased share of the company. It may be pointed out that section 113 of Indian Companies Act, 1956 is more or less same as section 108 of the Companies Act, 1913, with some minor variations and with an addition of sub-section (3) as quoted in paragraph 3 of that judgment. 

 9. In the present case, it is admitted that the accused petitioners completed the share certificates and made them ready for delivery within time. But instead of delivering the same to the complainant they mortgaged the same to BSRS for raising loan without the consent of the complainant and as such they allegedly committed an offence as contemplated under section 108(2) of the Companies Act. 

 11. We have already found that the petitioners are to complete the share certificates and make them ready for delivery within 3 months. In the present case it is not the complainant's case that share certificates of the complainant were not made ready within 3 months. Once the share certificates are completed and made ready within time, the liability of the accused persons, in our opinion, ends. The law does not provide that after the direction of the Court they are to make the share certificates again ready for delivery to the complainant. 

 12. In view of above, we arc of opinion that the principles of law enunciated in the above reported case is applicable in the facts of the present case and the accused petitioners did not commit any offence within the meaning of section 108 (2) of the Companies Act, 1913 by not delivering the share certificates to the complainant in the facts and circumstances of the present case. It may be pointed out that the complainant has already obtained a decree with respect to the non-delivery of the share certificates which has already been upheld up to the Appellate Division. His remedy lies in executing the decree in the Civil Court and not in the Criminal Court. 

 14. Mr. SC Das, the learned Advocate for the opposite party, on the other hand, contends that the fine mentioned in section 108 (2) of the Companies Act is also an offence. In support of his contention he referred to the case of Harish Chandra Vs. Kavindra Narain Sina and others, reported in AIR (1936) (All) (FB) at page 830 where it has been held as follows: 

 15. Dr. Rafiqur Rahman, the learned Advocate for the petitioners, on the other hand, argues that the facts of the above case are quite different from the facts of the present case. He submits that the liability of the unqualified directors is a personal liability of the person who acts as director without having the requisite qualification to act as a director and, as such, the principle of law enunciated in that case is not applicable in the facts of present casco In any view of matter, as we have held that non-delivery of the share certificates to the complainant is not an offence under section 108 (2) of the Companies Act, we are of opinion that the proceeding is liable to be quashed. 

 In view of above, the application is allowed and the rule is made absolute. The impugned proceeding of the Petition Case No. 345 A-1/89 pending in the Court of Chief Metropolitan Magistrate, Dhaka is hereby quashed.
